pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–11 years

- **Topic:** Eruption Types & Volcano Shape — eruptions range from gentle (effusive lava flows) to violently explosive, depending on the magma's properties (thickness/stickiness and gas content), and volcano SHAPE follows from eruption style.

- **Standards — UK (KS2, mixed placement):** KS2 **Geography** enrichment (physical geography: volcanoes); the material-properties reasoning (viscosity, gas) links loosely to KS2 science 'states/properties of materials' but the volcanic detail is beyond the statutory KS2 science. Frame via Geography + a properties-of-magma lens.

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** No dedicated elementary PE; volcanic processes and Earth materials are middle-school (**MS-ESS2** / **MS-ESS3-2** hazards). The property→behaviour reasoning is a strong cause-and-effect (CCC) exercise. State-standard tier: DEFERRED.

- **Operational details:** Prerequisites 'Inside a Volcano' and 'Active/Dormant/Extinct'. Deliver a two-variable causal chain: magma that is THIN and runny with little gas → gas escapes easily → gentle effusive lava flows → broad, gently-sloping SHIELD volcano; magma that is THICK/sticky and gas-rich → gas is trapped and pressure builds → violent EXPLOSIVE eruption of ash and rock → steep cone/composite volcano. The load-bearing idea: the SAME underground plumbing gives wildly different eruptions and shapes because of the magma's properties — shape is a clue to eruption style.
bestPractices: Foreground the causal variables (thickness/stickiness + gas) and treat eruption style and shape as their CONSEQUENCES, not as unrelated categories.

Use a viscosity + trapped-gas analogy children can feel: runny water/syrup vs thick honey/ketchup; gas escaping from a gently-opened fizzy drink vs a shaken one (thin lets gas out gently; thick traps it → explosive).
Link shape to style directly: runny lava spreads far → wide low shield; sticky lava piles near the vent + ash layers → steep cone — so you can 'read' a volcano's shape.
Contrast real archetypes (Hawaiian shield eruptions vs Vesuvius/Mount St Helens explosive) so both ends of the spectrum are concrete.
Emphasise it is a spectrum, not two boxes, and that explosive isn't 'more lava' — it's trapped gas releasing suddenly.
keyRepresentations: A magma 'thickness' (viscosity) scale and a 'gas content' scale, each linked to an eruption outcome
Fizzy-drink analogy: gently opened (thin, gas escapes) vs shaken/thick (gas trapped → explosion)
Paired cross-sections: broad shield from runny lava vs steep layered cone from sticky/ashy eruptions
Shield vs composite/cinder-cone shape gallery linked to eruption style
commonMisconceptions: All volcanoes erupt the same way (runny flows) or all explode (eruption style spans a spectrum set by magma properties).
Explosive eruptions happen because there is MORE lava (they happen because thick, sticky magma traps gas until pressure releases suddenly).
Volcano shape is random or just cosmetic (shape is a direct consequence of eruption style — it's evidence).
Lava is always fast-flowing and deadly to outrun (thin lava can flow far; thick magma often barely flows but erupts explosively — the ash/blast is the danger).
Gas has nothing to do with eruptions (dissolved gas coming out of magma is the main driver of explosivity).

learn.summary: For ages 9–11, teach that volcanic eruptions span a spectrum from gentle effusive lava flows to violently explosive ash blasts, driven by two magma properties — thickness/stickiness (viscosity) and dissolved gas content — and that a volcano's shape is a readable consequence of its eruption style: runny, low-gas magma builds broad, low shield volcanoes; thick, gas-rich magma builds steep explosive cones. Load-bearing idea: the same underground plumbing yields very different eruptions and shapes because of the magma's properties, so shape is a clue to how a volcano erupts. The activities move from a manipulable two-variable model, through paired cross-section reference, a hands-on fizzy/syrup investigation, to consolidation and categorisation.

activities.title: Eruption workshop: dial the magma, watch style and shape change
feedback: If a learner expects 'more lava = bigger explosion', show that thick, gas-rich magma barely flows yet erupts far more violently: explosivity comes from trapped gas releasing suddenly, not from the amount of lava.
When a learner sets runny + low-gas and sees a wide low shield build up, prompt: 'Why did it spread so wide and stay low?' → thin lava flows far before cooling.
When thick + high-gas produces a steep cone and ash column, prompt: 'Where did the gas go in the runny case, and why couldn't it escape here?' to surface the trapped-gas driver.
If a learner treats it as two fixed boxes, have them try a middle setting to show it is a spectrum.
activities.rationale: A two-variable cause→effect system is well suited to live controls and recompute: manipulating thickness and gas and seeing both eruption style and final shape change makes the causal chain concrete. A dynamic model can show the inputs changing and the outputs recomputing, which a single still image does not animate; this is an affordance of the interaction, not evidence it teaches better than the cross-section or hands-on alternatives. OPTIONAL interaction examples (two sliders/dials, predict-then-run, profile building up over repeated eruptions, tagging real volcanoes at matching settings) make the mechanism tangible but are not mandatory.
sourceClaims: Eruption style (effusive vs explosive) depends chiefly on magma viscosity and dissolved gas content; runny low-gas magma builds shield volcanoes, sticky gas-rich magma builds steep explosive composite cones.
learnerActions: Set two controls: how THICK the magma is (runny → sticky) and how much GAS it holds (low → high).
Before running, PREDICT what will happen: gentle ooze or violent ash blast? Flat volcano or steep one?
Run the eruption and watch the outcome on a spectrum from oozing lava flow to explosive ash column.
Repeat eruptions and watch the volcano's profile build up over time into either a broad low shield or a steep composite cone.
Try the opposite extreme (e.g. thin+low-gas, then thick+high-gas) and compare how the SAME setup becomes a very different volcano just by changing the magma.
Match real volcanoes (e.g. Hawaiian shields vs Mount St Helens / Vesuvius) to the control settings that produce their style.
activities.intendedInsight: Eruption style and volcano shape are both consequences of two magma properties — thickness and gas content — not separate or random categories; a volcano's shape is evidence of how it erupts.

activities.title: Paired cross-sections: read why one is steep and one is flat
feedback: If a learner says the steep one is steep 'because it's bigger', point to the layers of ash and sticky lava piled near the vent versus far-spreading runny flows.
Reinforce the full chain: name the magma property, then the style, then the shape it builds.
activities.rationale: Paired labelled cross-sections present the property→style→shape mapping clearly and make durable reference material. They show the end states rather than letting the learner vary the inputs, so they pair well with the manipulable workshop rather than replacing it.
sourceClaims: Eruption style (effusive vs explosive) depends chiefly on magma viscosity and dissolved gas content; runny low-gas magma builds shield volcanoes, sticky gas-rich magma builds steep explosive composite cones.
learnerActions: Study two labelled volcano cross-sections side by side: a broad shield and a steep layered composite cone.
Reveal, for each, the magma properties (runny + low-gas vs sticky + gas-rich), the eruption style, and a real example.
Answer the lift-the-flap question 'Why is this one steep and that one flat?' and check against the revealed cause.
Describe in your own words how runny lava spreads to make a wide shield while sticky lava and ash pile near the vent to make a steep cone.
activities.intendedInsight: The mapping property → eruption style → shape can be read off a volcano's cross-section; shape is built up by the kind of eruptions, not decorative.

activities.title: Thin vs thick 'magma': a hands-on fizz investigation
feedback: If a learner predicts both will behave the same, or that 'more liquid matters', discuss what the bottles actually showed. Use the thickness-and-trapped-gas idea to explain it, and if the result was unclear or unexpected, discuss why (for example, slow mixing in syrup). Then link back to the model: in real magma, it is thickness and trapped gas, not the amount of magma, that mainly decide how violent an eruption is.
Connect back: the syrup is like sticky, gas-rich magma; the water is like runny, low-gas magma.
activities.rationale: A concrete physical investigation lets learners predict, observe and feel the trapped-gas mechanism (a viscosity + trapped-gas analogy), which supports the causal model behind effusive vs explosive eruptions. This is an analogy for magma behaviour, not a literal model of volcanic chemistry.
sourceClaims: Eruption style (effusive vs explosive) depends chiefly on magma viscosity and dissolved gas content; runny low-gas magma builds shield volcanoes, sticky gas-rich magma builds steep explosive composite cones.
learnerActions: Set up two clear bottles: one of water, one of thick syrup or honey, each with a little bicarbonate of soda.
Before adding vinegar, PREDICT which will 'erupt' more violently when gas forms — and say WHY.

Add the same amount of vinegar to each (over a tray, bottles left open) and record what you actually see. Look for whether bubbles escape quickly from the runny water, and whether the thick syrup holds bubbles in a rising foam that pushes up and out. Results can vary: in thick syrup the vinegar mixes in slowly, so it may fizz less. Write down what happened rather than what you expected.

Compare a fizzy drink opened gently with one that has been shaken (adult-supervised, over a tray). Both are the same thin liquid, so this is not a thick-vs-thin test. It shows how gas dissolved under pressure can rush out suddenly when the pressure is released, like gas coming out of rising magma.
Using what you observed, say which bottle is the better model of effusive (runny) magma and which of explosive (thick) magma. Explain why, and name one way the bottles are not like real magma.
activities.intendedInsight: Thick magma traps gas so pressure builds and releases suddenly (explosive), while thin magma lets gas escape gently (effusive) — the violence comes from trapped gas, not the amount of liquid.

activities.title: Consolidate and sort: match properties, style and shape
feedback: When a learner picks the 'more lava' answer, re-explain that explosivity is trapped gas releasing suddenly, independent of how much lava there is.
If a learner ties violence to volcano size, note that even a small vent can erupt explosively if the magma is thick and gas-rich.
activities.rationale: The clean property→style→shape mapping supports consolidation through matching, categorisation and reasoning questions. These tasks check whether the learner can apply the causal rule; use them after the model and investigation so they test an understood mechanism rather than isolated labels. A sort can check whether a learner classifies volcanoes correctly, but it does not by itself elicit the explanation, so the added 'say what magma produced it' step is included.
sourceClaims: Eruption style (effusive vs explosive) depends chiefly on magma viscosity and dissolved gas content; runny low-gas magma builds shield volcanoes, sticky gas-rich magma builds steep explosive composite cones.
learnerActions: Match each magma description (thin+low-gas / thick+gas-rich) to its eruption style and resulting volcano shape.
Sort a set of volcano images into shield vs steep cone, and for each say what magma likely produced it.
Answer 'Why do some volcanoes explode?' choosing between a correct trapped-gas explanation and a wrong 'because there is more lava' option.
Answer 'Could a small volcano still have a violent explosive eruption?' and justify using magma properties, not size.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can apply the rule — magma properties decide eruption style, and style builds shape — and reject size or amount of lava as the cause of explosivity.

constraints: Prerequisites: 'Inside a Volcano' (the underground plumbing) and 'Active/Dormant/Extinct' before this topic.
Teach eruption style as a SPECTRUM, not two boxes: effusive and explosive are ends of a range set by magma properties.

Explosive eruptions are NOT caused by more lava. In this topic they are explained by thick, gas-rich magma trapping gas until the pressure is released suddenly (other triggers, such as magma meeting water, exist but are beyond this topic). Keep this distinction front and centre.
Volcano shape is a consequence of eruption style (evidence), not decorative or random.
Correct the common 'lava is always fast and deadly to outrun' idea: thin lava can flow far, while thick magma often barely flows but erupts explosively — the ash and blast are the main danger.
The fizzy-drink and syrup/water investigation are ANALOGIES for magma viscosity and trapped gas, not literal volcanic chemistry; make the analogy's purpose explicit.

Matching/categorisation and multiple-choice tasks check recognition and application of the rule; they do not by themselves require the learner to manipulate the variables or produce an explanation, so use them to consolidate after hands-on and model-based work.
A rotatable 3D shield-vs-cone comparison is an optional extension; 2D profiles already convey the shape–style link, so 3D is polish rather than a requirement.

Curriculum placement: in England, volcanoes are named statutory content in KS2 Geography (physical geography), and this topic's magma-property reasoning extends beyond that. Any link to materials-properties reasoning goes beyond statutory KS2 science. In NGSS, Grade 4 covers volcanoes through patterns of Earth features (4-ESS2-2) and reducing natural-hazard impacts (4-ESS3-2), while the magma-property and eruption-style reasoning fits better with middle school (MS-ESS2 / MS-ESS3).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy entry asserted that the dynamic 'change a property, watch style and shape change' insight is one 'no static image can give'. This comparative necessity is not established by the cited sources; it has been reframed as an affordance of manipulable models (which animate changing inputs/outputs), and the paired cross-section and hands-on alternatives are preserved as genuinely useful, not merely inferior.
Source claims are marked verified:false in the row; the central USGS-attributed claim about viscosity and dissolved gas driving eruption style is standard geology but has not been re-verified here.

Self-audit: the property→style→shape causal chain, the 'explosivity = trapped gas, not amount of lava' point, the spectrum framing, and the lava-danger clarification were checked for internal consistency across summary, insights, actions and feedback and retained; no arithmetic or force/motion content is present to correct. Quiz-step vocabulary ('distractor') was removed from all learner-facing text.

assess.poeTask: Give the child two clear bottles: one of water, one of thick syrup or honey, each with a little bicarbonate of soda, plus vinegar to add. Before adding the vinegar, ask them to PREDICT which will 'erupt' more violently when the gas forms — and WHY. Many predict the same for both, or that 'more liquid' matters. What happens: the runny water lets the gas fizz out gently, while the thick syrup traps the bubbles so pressure builds and it bursts out — mimicking runny (effusive) vs thick (explosive) magma. The reason given before adding the vinegar reveals whether they connect an eruption's violence to the magma's THICKNESS and trapped gas rather than to its amount or the volcano's size.
probeDeeper: Why does thick, sticky magma tend to explode while runny magma flows gently?
What part does gas dissolved in the magma play in how violent an eruption is?
Could a small volcano still have a violent explosive eruption? Why?
Why is a shield volcano wide and low but an ash-cone steep?
assess.correctAnswer: It's not about size. Runny (thin) magma with little gas lets gas escape easily, so it erupts gently as lava flows and builds a wide, low shield volcano; thick, sticky magma traps gas until it bursts out violently with ash and rock, building a steep-sided cone. The magma's thickness and gas content decide the eruption style, and the style builds the shape.

errorPatterns.pattern: The difference is just the volcano's size (bigger = more explosive)
errorPatterns.nextMove: It's the magma's thickness and gas, not size; even a small vent can erupt violently.
errorPatterns.distractor: It's just how big each volcano is — bigger ones explode more.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Explains eruption violence by how big the volcano is.

errorPatterns.pattern: All volcanoes erupt the same violent, explosive way
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast a gentle Hawaiian lava flow with an explosive ash blast — the magma differs.
errorPatterns.distractor: All volcanoes erupt the same violent way.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Assumes every eruption is a big blast.

errorPatterns.pattern: The volcano's shape is just how it looks — not caused by the eruptions
errorPatterns.nextMove: The shape is BUILT UP by the kind of eruptions — runny lava spreads wide, thick lava and ash pile up steep.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats the shape as decorative or random, not built by eruption style.

responseLevels.gap: Attributes eruption style to size or chance; thinks all volcanoes erupt alike.
responseLevels.full: Explains runny low-gas magma erupts gently (wide shield) while thick gas-rich magma erupts explosively (steep cone) — magma properties decide the style, and the style builds the shape.
responseLevels.partial: Contrasts gentle vs explosive eruptions and knows magma matters, but can't tie thickness+gas to the style, or can't connect style to shape.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Two volcanoes: one is a wide, gently-sloping mound that oozes runny lava; the other is a steep cone that blasts out ash and rock. A friend says the difference is just how big each volcano is. Is that right? What actually decides whether an eruption is a gentle flow or a violent explosion — and how does that shape the volcano?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child can name effusive/explosive yet attribute the difference to size or luck. Asking what DECIDES the style forces the magma-thickness-and-gas variable, and the shape-as-consequence — separating a causal model from surface labels.
